title: Will and Parish
premise: Felix Pemberton, the meticulous estate lawyer of the small town of Marrow's Bend, is reading the will of matriarch Edith Vane when a second will surfaces—one dated after her death, impossible on its face, naming Felix as executor of a fortune that doesn't exist. A confession letter postmarked the day after the funeral points to a ledger hidden in plain sight in the town library's card catalog, one that records twenty years of bribes, cover-ups, and a drowning everyone agreed to forget. As Felix decodes the ledger with Edith's estranged granddaughter June, they discover the town's most beloved citizens engineered a death and paid Felix—unknowingly—to bury the evidence. In the end, Felix must choose between the law they've served and the justice Edith demanded from beyond the grave: they burn nothing, publish everything, and hand the ledger to a state investigator, shattering the town but freeing themselves from ten years of complicit silence.
about_author: Hazel Reyes is a former small-town paralegal who spent a decade watching secrets move through probate files before turning them into fiction. She writes mysteries about paper trails and the people who keep them, from a farmhouse office full of dead clients' filing cabinets.

chapters.title: The Reading
chapters.summary: Felix Pemberton's POV. Felix reads Edith Vane's will to a packed parlor of expectant heirs, everything precise as always—until a second envelope appears in the file, sealed in Edith's handwriting, dated three days after her death. The emotional beat is professional composure cracking into quiet dread.

chapters.title: Postmarked Yesterday
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. The impossible will names Felix executor of an unnamed asset and arrives by mail postmarked the day after the funeral. June Vane, the estranged granddaughter, shows up unannounced demanding answers. Beat: unease deepening into suspicion that someone is playing a long game with Felix at the center.

chapters.title: Ten Years Alphabetized
chapters.summary: Felix's POV, with flashback. We learn how Felix came to Marrow's Bend, built a practice on discretion, and quietly filed away the town's ugliest secrets without ever reading them twice. Beat: guilt surfacing—Felix realizes discretion was always another word for complicity.

chapters.title: What June Remembers
chapters.summary: June's POV. June recalls her grandmother's final phone call—cut off mid-sentence, mentioning 'the drawer' and a boy who drowned. She doesn't trust Felix, assuming the lawyer is part of whatever silenced Edith. Beat: wary alliance formed out of mutual need rather than trust.

chapters.title: The Card Catalog
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Following the confession letter's cryptic reference, Felix searches the town library and finds a card catalog entry for a book that was never cataloged—a hollow drawer containing the first page of a ledger written in Edith's shorthand. Beat: thrill of discovery shadowed by fear of what the ledger will say.

chapters.title: A Boy Named Danny
chapters.summary: June's POV. The first decoded entries point to 2004 and the drowning of Danny Okafor, ruled an accident, mourned by the whole town—including the sheriff, the pastor, and Felix's own mentor. Beat: grief and horror as a childhood memory becomes evidence of murder.

chapters.title: The Sheriff's Courtesy Call
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Sheriff Dale Pruitt visits Felix's office, friendly and chilling, reminding Felix how much the town has done for them and asking pointed questions about 'Edith's little projects.' Beat: menace wrapped in neighborliness; Felix understands they are being watched.

chapters.title: Entries in Red Ink
chapters.summary: June's POV. Decoding accelerates: red-inked entries record payments—hush money routed through the church renovation fund, the school board, Felix's own firm. June confronts Felix about the payments made to their office. Beat: betrayal; the alliance nearly breaks.

chapters.title: Mentor's Drawer
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Felix searches the files of deceased mentor Harold Finch and finds matching ledgers—Harold was Edith's co-recordkeeper, or her rival. A note in Harold's hand warns: 'She keeps the truth; we keep the peace.' Beat: Felix realizes the conspiracy had two archivists, and only one wanted it exposed.

chapters.title: The Pastor's Sermon
chapters.summary: June's POV. At Sunday service, Reverend Lyle Marsh preaches on forgiveness and moving forward, staring directly at June. Afterward he offers her 'help' leaving town. Beat: open threat delivered as grace; June refuses and knows she's marked.

chapters.title: Fire at the Firm
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. A fire guts Felix's office overnight, destroying client files—but Felix, increasingly paranoid, had moved the ledgers home. The fire is ruled electrical. Beat: escalation from intimidation to violence; no more illusions about what the town will do.

chapters.title: Danny's Mother
chapters.summary: June's POV. The two track down Ruth Okafor, living at the edge of town, who has waited twenty years for someone to ask. She gives them Danny's last letter, describing what he saw at the quarry the night he died. Beat: righteous anger transformed into purpose; the case gains a human face.

chapters.title: The Quarry at Night
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Felix and June search the quarry site named in Danny's letter and find a rusted toolbox wedged in the rocks—inside, physical proof tying Sheriff Pruitt and businessman Cole Vane, Edith's son, to the scene. Beat: dread solidifying into certainty, and the terrible knowledge that Cole is June's father.

chapters.title: Father and Daughter
chapters.summary: June's POV. June confronts Cole privately, giving him a chance to confess before she goes public. He admits presence but claims the sheriff acted alone—and threatens her with disinheritance and worse. Beat: heartbreak; June severs the last tie to her family name.

chapters.title: Harold's Last Client
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Digging through Harold's effects, Felix finds a letter Harold wrote before his suspicious heart attack: proof that Edith witnessed the killing and traded silence for leverage, keeping the ledger as insurance—which is why she died. Beat: moral vertigo; even their victim was complicit.

chapters.title: The Second Will Explained
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Felix finally understands: Edith dictated the posthumous will before dying, trusting only the mail and time. The 'asset' is the truth itself, and the executor's duty is publication. Beat: reluctant acceptance of the inheritance—Felix was chosen precisely because they kept everyone's secrets.

chapters.title: Cornered at the Bend
chapters.summary: June's POV. With the ledger copied and hidden, June is run off the road near the bend where Danny died. She escapes into the woods, injured, and calls Felix from a payphone—the first place she can think of that feels safe. Beat: terror and trust converging; the alliance becomes devotion.

chapters.title: Confessions in the Parlor
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Felix summons the conspirators—Pruitt, Marsh, Cole—to the office under pretext of settling the estate, records their guarded admissions, and reveals the ledger exists. Pruitt draws his weapon. Beat: climax ignites; words become weapons in a room full of guilty men.

chapters.title: What the Law Can't Do
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Standoff resolved when Ruth Okafor arrives with a state investigator Edith had contacted months before her death—Felix's recorded confessions and the ledger give him jurisdiction outside the town's reach. Arrests begin. Beat: catharsis; justice arrives not through loyalty to the town but betrayal of it.

chapters.title: The Funerals They Attend
chapters.summary: June's POV. Cole dies by suicide awaiting trial; the town fractures between those who knew and those who didn't want to. June buries her father beside a grandmother she's only now beginning to understand. Beat: sorrow without absolution; belonging redefined as chosen, not inherited.

chapters.title: Probate of a Town
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Months later: trials underway, the firm rebuilt with Ruth Okafor as partner, the ledger entered into evidence and read aloud in court. Felix drafts Edith's true estate distribution—her fortune to Danny's family and the library. Beat: restitution; the alphabetized secrets finally sorted into light.

chapters.title: Will and Parish
chapters.summary: Alternating POV, closing scene. Felix and June place a new card in the library catalog: a real book, Danny's story, properly filed. The confession letter's last line—'truth is the only will that executes itself'—is engraved on a bench by the quarry. Beat: quiet resolution; loyalty survived by being redirected toward the truth.
